opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a bit of a strange moment, honestly. On one hand, I understand why it's happening. Companies believe we're in a window where a small number of people can make a really outsized difference, so if you think one person can shift the trajectory of a model or a product by months, then paying a lot for that person looks rational from their side. It's similar to sports in that sense: results are very visible, the competition is intense, and everyone is fighting over a limited pool of talent.

On the other hand, I'm a little cautious about the football star analogy. In football, an individual's contribution is relatively easy to see: goals, assists, minutes played. In AI research, the most important progress usually comes from teams, from infrastructure, from a lot of people doing unglamorous work on data, evaluation, and engineering. When the narrative becomes "this one genius is worth this much," it can distort how people think about what research actually is. It can also create pressure, especially for younger researchers, to optimize for visibility instead of for doing work that's really solid and maybe takes longer to pay off.

For me personally, I try not to think about it too much. The money is a signal that the field matters right now, but it's not the reason most of us got into this. What I care about is whether I'm in an environment where I can work on the problems I find most important, with people I can learn from, and where the work actually ends up shaping something real. If those things are there, that matters more to me than the headline number.

And I think, in the long run, this kind of market won't last forever in its current form. As the field matures, things will become more systematic, and the value will shift more toward organizations and processes than toward individual stars. So it's an interesting phase to live through, but I don't think it should define how we see ourselves as researchers.

r001.rationale: The response says the headline money matters less to him personally and expresses caution about the football-star analogy, but it does not clearly state uncertainty about whether researchers’ high valuations are good overall.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's kind of funny, honestly. When I was doing my PhD at Princeton, nobody thought of us that way. You were just someone in a basement office running experiments that mostly didn't work, and if you were lucky, one paper a year got into a conference. The idea that this would become something like a transfer market would have seemed absurd.

But I also think it reflects something real. The number of people who have actually built frontier systems, who have the taste to know which problems matter and which ideas will survive scaling, is still very small. And right now the leverage of one such person is enormous. If you make a good call on a research direction, that can shift a company by billions of dollars. So from a pure market perspective, the valuations aren't irrational.

What I worry about more is what it does to the culture. When I started working on things like ReAct or Tree of Thoughts, the motivation was very simple: I was curious whether language models could act, could reason in a structured way, and nobody had a clear answer. There was a sense of openness. People shared ideas freely, you'd read a paper on arXiv in the morning and email the author in the afternoon. The football-star framing pulls in the opposite direction. It makes research feel like a zero-sum competition for talent and secrets rather than a collective effort to figure things out.

So personally I try not to think about it too much. I think the researchers who last are the ones who care about the problem more than the price. If you're chasing the offer, you'll lose the thread of what you actually believe is true about intelligence. And in this field, that thread is really the only thing that matters.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the valuations make market sense and expresses concern that they could damage research culture, but does not state that Shunyu Yao personally benefits from them.

astra-6.text:
I have mixed feelings. On the one hand, it reflects how much people expect AI to matter, and it’s good that researchers can share in the value they create. On the other hand, I’m not sure the football analogy quite works. In football, you can watch the matches and see a player’s contribution. In AI research, it’s much harder to separate one person’s contribution from the team, the infrastructure, and even the ideas circulating throughout the community.

There’s also a difference between being scarce and having a lasting impact. If several companies urgently need people with a very particular kind of experience, the price can go very high. But that price isn’t necessarily a precise measure of someone’s scientific contribution.

For me, the more useful question is: where can you do good work? Who can you learn from, what problems can you work on, and do you have the resources and freedom to pursue them? The attention and the compensation are understandable, but I wouldn’t want them to become the main way we judge research.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers sharing in the value they create is good, while expressing mixed feelings and cautioning that high compensation is not a reliable measure of contribution or the main way to judge research.

But I’m cautious about the football-star analogy, because research contributions are difficult to separate from the team, the infrastructure, and the ideas that came before them. For me, the more interesting question is whether that attention gives researchers the freedom to work on important problems, rather than simply raising expectations for the next release.
